fit: incident psychosis after minor phenomena in a selected Parkinson cohort
assessment: The prospective cohort followed people with baseline minor phenomena, including illusions, feelings of presence and passage hallucinations. Of 38 recruited, 34 entered the primary analysis and 24 developed psychosis during follow-up. Time to onset on the MDS-UPDRS and enhanced SAPS-PD is a composite incident outcome, with no dried fig intake measurement or food-specific visual episode rate.

fit: atypical parkinsonism protocol with planned diet and clinical phenotyping
assessment: ATPARK plans collection of food habits and environmental risk factors, along with longitudinal clinical phenotyping across atypical parkinsonism syndromes. Visual hallucinations appear in the literature discussion of phenotypes. The protocol does not identify a dried fig item or an outcome estimate linked to food intake.

fit: cognitive fluctuation instrument in Parkinson disease without dementia
assessment: The article assesses the Dementia Cognitive Fluctuation Scale in people with Parkinson disease without dementia. The investigators distinguish fluctuations of attention or arousal and discuss visual hallucinations as part of the clinical background. Scale performance and correlates are separate from the effect of eating dried figs on visual hallucinations.

fit: withdrawal drug study with composite relapse and shared HARMONY registration
assessment: A post hoc HARMONY subgroup analysis evaluates continued pimavanserin versus randomized withdrawal in selected responders with Parkinson disease dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies. Relapse occurred in 1 of 19 continuing drug and 11 of 20 on placebo in the interim efficacy set. The endpoint combines hallucinations and delusions with other relapse criteria, and there is no food exposure. The subgroup is part of NCT03325556.

fit: meal timing in a blood pressure case series with cognitive outcomes
assessment: The series links caregiver-recorded cognitive fluctuations in four people with Parkinson disease dementia to immediately preceding low blood pressure on ambulatory monitoring. Meal timing appears in the plots and the authors propose more detailed food documentation in future studies. Visual hallucinations are recorded in case histories, rather than as the events associated with meals. No fig is identified and the study gives no comparable visual episode frequency.

fit: visually elicited event counts and clinical-history groups
assessment: In eleven participants, the controlled VR procedure records 17 misperceptions and six visual hallucinations. The counts come from the laboratory setting. No dried fig comparison or naturalistic duration measurement follows a dietary exposure.

fit: temporally observed changes in alertness and blood pressure
assessment: The case records regained alertness after change in body position and blood pressure. Visual hallucinations appear in the history as a separate manifestation. There is no dried fig timing or event rate.

fit: blood pressure variability and cross-sectional Parkinson hallucinations or psychosis
assessment: The combined item or treated psychosis definition classified 46 of 121 Parkinson participants. An association between that group and blood pressure variability does not identify the frequency of visual episodes or any food exposure.

fit: pure autonomic failure with visual misidentification and glucose-associated hypotension
assessment: The original distinguishes a reported visual misidentification from a recorded glucose challenge and blood pressure drop. The clinical diagnosis and endpoints do not substantiate a relation between dried figs and Parkinson visual episodes.

fit: genetic proxy for generic dried fruit and diagnosis risk
assessment: The analysis reports a positive relation with diagnosis risk for a broad UK Biobank dried-fruit exposure. A diagnosis endpoint, broad exposure instrument and genetic proxy do not measure visual symptom frequency after dried fig intake.

fit: abstract-depth comparison for grouped dried fruit and diagnosis risk
assessment: The publisher abstract reports a generic dried-fruit risk association for Parkinson diagnosis. It does not distinguish figs, individual clinical symptoms or independence from earlier genetic exposure inputs. Main tables remain open.

fit: Dutch three-day dietary diary and microbiome outcomes
assessment: The Dutch DUPARC cohort records nutrients with a three-day diary for microbiome covariate adjustment. Public sequences are linked. Original meals and visual hallucination events are not linked in the publication.

fit: diet-history questionnaire and Parkinson microbiome composition
assessment: The published predictors are aggregate diet quality, fiber and added sugar and the outcomes concern microbial profiles. A specific dried fig intake and clinical visual episode rate remain unreported.

fit: multiethnic dietary habits and broad perception domain
assessment: The observational analysis includes fresh fruit as a food class and describes its combined NMSS perception and hallucination domain. Its author-reported corrected comparisons concern selected patterns, supplements and herbs or beverages and provide no result by dried fig and visual episode frequency.
